Your reels, their rules A meme creator lost his posts, then his Instagram account, over copyright complaints, with no notice and no hearing. The Madhya Pradesh High Court has upheld the rule that allowed it. What can creators do? Rule 3(1)(b)(iv) Grievance appeal Creator checklist Adv. What happened The creator A meme page with about 39,000 followers, and a source of income. July and August 2025 Posts removed after third-party copyright complaints. No notice, no hearing. The account Suspended. He used the grievance process and sought reinstatement, without success. The challenge He argued Rule 3(1)(b)(iv) of the IT Rules lets a private company decide infringement, a job for courts, in breach of Articles 14, 19 and 21. 17 September 2026 Petition dismissed (Chief Justice Kogje and Justice Rusia). Reported 27 October. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 02 / 08

The rule stands 1 Instagram is an intermediary under s. 2(w) of the IT Act, with due-diligence duties, including acting against infringing content. 2 It can run its platform. Once the law lets a private company operate as an intermediary, it may manage and control its service. 3 The safeguards are enough: a grievance officer (Rule 3(2)) and an appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee (Rule 3A). 4 Other routes exist under Chapters IX and X of the IT Act (adjudication and appeal). Adv. Ashwani Kumar 03 / 08

YOUR REMEDIES, IN ORDER If your post or account is removed Platform appeal IMMEDIATELY 1 Use the in-app "disagree" or dispute option. Ask who complained and about what. Grievance Officer · Rule 3(2) 24 H / 15 DAYS 2 Must acknowledge within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days. Grievance Appellate Committee · Rule WITHIN 30 DAYS 3 3A Appeal online at gac.gov.in. The GAC aims to decide within 30 days. Courts and other forums THEN 4 IT Act adjudication or a civil suit against a bad-faith claimant. A writ against the platform itself is now harder. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 04 / 08

THE GAP Who decides what infringes? COPYRIGHT RULES, 2013 · RULE 75 A built-in check The complainant must identify the work and its ownership, and say the use isn't fair dealing. The platform acts only if satisfied. If no court order comes within 21 days, the content may be restored. IN PRACTICE Platform policy decides Claims are processed at scale and users often don't see the complaint. Memes and reviews may be fair dealing for criticism or review under s. 52(1)(a), but a platform team makes that call, not a judge. THE SHARPEST EDGE Losing the whole account Removing one post is targeted. Suspending an account built over years, often a livelihood, is a far heavier step. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 05 / 08

Right on takedowns, too light on process 1 Platforms must act on infringement. The court is right that rights-holders need a working remedy. 2 But tell the creator. The complaint, the claimant and the work said to be copied, with a chance to respond. 3 Proportionality. Remove the post first; suspend the account only for repeat infringement, after warnings. 4 Deter false claims. Verify claimants, and act against those who misuse copyright to silence rivals or critics. 5 Make the GAC count. Publish its decisions and ensure platforms comply with them. Adv. TA K E AWAY On someone else's platform, your rights are mostly procedural. The ruling confirms that platforms can act on copyright complaints. Creators' protection now lies in using every step of the grievance ladder, keeping records, and pushing for fairer process: notice, proportion, and checks on false claims. Adv.
